extracted.intended_audience: graduate students and researchers in analysis/partial differential equations studying Sobolev spaces and variational methods for elliptic boundary value problems
extracted.subtask_description: Formulate, analyse, and solve second-order elliptic boundary value problems using Sobolev spaces and variational methods: define weak/classical solutions, establish existence/uniqueness (Lax–Milgram / minimization), study regularity and maximum principles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classical vs weak solution (Dirichlet Laplacian)
rubrics_metrics.description: Classical solution: u ∈ C^2(Ω) satisfying −Δu + u = f in Ω and u = 0 on ∂Ω. Weak solution: u ∈ H^1_0(Ω) satisfying ∫_Ω (∇u·∇v + u v) = ∫_Ω f v for all v ∈ H^1_0(Ω) (equation (32)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Every classical solution is a weak solution (use integration by parts); conversely one seeks u in H^1_0(Ω) satisfying the integral identity. Use density of C_c^1(Ω) in H^1_0(Ω) to extend identities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Existence and uniqueness via Lax–Milgram / Dirichlet principle
rubrics_metrics.description: Given f ∈ L^2(Ω) (Ω bounded), there exists a unique weak solution u ∈ H^1_0(Ω) of −Δu + u = f, and u is the minimizer of the energy functional ½∫(|∇v|^2+|v|^2) − ∫ f v over v ∈ H^1_0(Ω) (Theorem 9.21).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply Lax–Milgram in the Hilbert space H^1_0(Ω) with bilinear form a(u,v)=∫(∇u·∇v + u v) and linear functional v↦∫ f v. Coerciveness and continuity of a(·,·) provide existence and uniqueness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Weak formulation for inhomogeneous Dirichlet data
rubrics_metrics.description: If u = g on ∂Ω and there exists ˜g ∈ H^1(Ω) ∩ C(Ω) with trace g, set K={v∈H^1(Ω): v−˜g ∈ H^1_0(Ω)}. A weak solution is u ∈ K satisfying ∫(∇u·∇v + u v)=∫ f v for all v ∈ H^1_0(Ω) (equation (34)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: K is a nonempty closed convex subset of H^1(Ω). Equivalently u ∈ K satisfies the variational inequality ∫(∇u·(∇v−∇u)+u(v−u)) ≥ ∫ f (v−u) for all v∈K (equation (35)). Existence/uniqueness follow from minimization over K and Stampacchia's theorem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ellipticity condition for second-order operators
rubrics_metrics.description: The coefficient matrix (a_{ij}(x)) must satisfy a_{ij}(x) ξ_i ξ_j ≥ α |ξ|^2 for all x∈Ω, ξ∈R^N and some α>0 (equation (36)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This uniform positive-definiteness (ellipticity) is a standing hypothesis to obtain coerciveness (together with other hypotheses like a_0 ≥ 0 and Poincaré) and to deduce regularity. The condition is preserved under smooth changes of variables (Lemma 9.8).

rubrics_metrics.name: Weak formulation for general second-order elliptic equations
rubrics_metrics.description: For operators with coefficients a_{ij}, a_i, a_0, a weak solution u ∈ H^1_0(Ω) satisfies ∫_Ω (∑_{i,j} a_{ij} ∂_i u ∂_j v + ∑_i a_i ∂_i u v + a_0 u v) = ∫_Ω f v for all v ∈ H^1_0(Ω) (equation (38)/(40)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Define the associated bilinear form a(u,v) as in (41). Continuity of coefficients ensures continuity of a(·,·). Use Lax–Milgram when a(·,·) is coercive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coerciveness and use of Poincaré inequality
rubrics_metrics.description: Coerciveness of the bilinear form a(·,·) can be obtained from ellipticity of (a_{ij}), the condition a_0 ≥ 0, together with Poincaré's inequality on H^1_0(Ω).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Poincaré's inequality (Corollary 9.19) provides ∥u∥_{L^p} ≤ C ∥∇u∥_{L^p} for u∈W^{1,p}_0(Ω) when Ω bounded; thus the gradient seminorm is equivalent to the H^1_0-norm and gives coercivity needed for Lax–Milgram.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fredholm alternative and non-coercive problems
rubrics_metrics.description: For general non-coercive forms, the homogeneous equation may have a finite-dimensional space of solutions dimension d; (40) has a solution iff f satisfies d orthogonality conditions (Theorem 9.23).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Introduce a large λ>0 to make a(·,·)+λ(·,·) coercive, define the compact operator T: L^2 → L^2, reduce to (I − λT)v = f and apply Fredholm's alternative to deduce solvability conditions and finite-dimensional kernel properties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classical vs weak solution (Neumann problem)
rubrics_metrics.description: Classical solution: u ∈ C^2(Ω) with ∂u/∂n = 0 on ∂Ω and −Δu + u = f in Ω. Weak solution: u ∈ H^1(Ω) satisfying ∫(∇u·∇v + u v) = ∫ f v for all v ∈ H^1(Ω) (equation (45)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Green's identity relates the strong and weak formulations. Existence/uniqueness follow by Lax–Milgram applied in H^1(Ω). Recovery of the Neumann boundary condition from the weak form uses boundary integrals (equation (46) and (47)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Boundary condition at infinity for unbounded domains
rubrics_metrics.description: For unbounded domains one imposes decay/boundary condition at infinity (e.g., u(x)→0 as |x|→∞), which translates at the weak level to membership u∈H^1 (or H^1_0) appropriate to the domain (Example 5).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose the function space (H^1(R^N), H^1_0(R^N_+), etc.) corresponding to the boundary/infinity conditions; then formulate the weak problem with test space equal to that Sobolev space.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characterizations of W^{1,p}(Ω) (Proposition 9.18)
rubrics_metrics.description: For a C^1 domain Ω and 1<p<∞ the following are equivalent: (i) u∈W^{1,p}(Ω); (ii) there exists C such that |∫_Ω u ∂_i φ| ≤ C ∥φ∥_{L^{p'}(Ω)} for all φ∈C^1_c(R^N); (iii) the zero-extension ¯u belongs to W^{1,p}(R^N) (with matching distributional derivatives).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use approximations by C^1_c(Ω) functions for (i)⇒(ii); deduce global extension membership for (ii)⇒(iii); and local charts/partition of unity for (iii)⇒(i). This gives practical tests to verify W^{1,p}-membership and to construct extensions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dual space representation W^{-1,p'} (Proposition 9.20)
rubrics_metrics.description: Any F∈W^{-1,p'}(Ω) can be represented as F(v)=∫_Ω f_0 v + ∑_{i=1}^N ∫_Ω f_i ∂_i v with f_0,f_1,...,f_N ∈ L^{p'}(Ω) and ∥F∥ = max_{0≤i≤N} ∥f_i∥_{L^{p'}}; if Ω bounded one can take f_0=0.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This decomposition characterizes distributional functionals of order one and provides a norm-equivalent description useful to check that a given linear functional belongs to the dual space.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poincaré inequality and norm equivalence (Corollary 9.19)
rubrics_metrics.description: If 1≤p<∞ and Ω bounded open, there exists C(Ω,p) such that ∥u∥_{L^p(Ω)} ≤ C ∥∇u∥_{L^p(Ω)} for all u∈W^{1,p}_0(Ω); hence ∥∇u∥_{L^p} is a norm on W^{1,p}_0(Ω) equivalent to the full W^{1,p}-norm.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is used to get coercivity in variational problems and to treat ∥∇u∥ as the primary control quantity in H^1_0 or W^{1,p}_0.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regularity theorem for Dirichlet problem (Theorem 9.25)
rubrics_metrics.description: If Ω is C^2 with bounded boundary and f∈L^2(Ω), and u∈H^1_0(Ω) satisfies the weak Dirichlet problem, then u∈H^2(Ω) with ∥u∥_{H^2} ≤ C ∥f∥_{L^2}; more generally if Ω is C^{m+2} and f∈H^m then u∈H^{m+2} and corresponding estimates hold; if Ω and f are C^∞ then u∈C^∞ (Theorem 9.25).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regularity is obtained locally (interior regularity and boundary regularity) by flattening the boundary with charts, applying difference-quotient/translation methods, and using ellipticity. For m>N/2, H^{m+2} embeds into C^2 so u becomes classical.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regularity theorem for Neumann problem (Theorem 9.26)
rubrics_metrics.description: Under the same smoothness hypotheses as Theorem 9.25, the weak Neumann solution u∈H^1(Ω) satisfying the Neumann weak form belongs to H^2(Ω) (and higher regularity analogues hold) with the same type of estimates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof and estimates are analogous to the Dirichlet case (use local charts, translations in tangential directions, and ellipticity).

rubrics_metrics.name: Method of translations / difference quotients for regularity
rubrics_metrics.description: Use difference quotients D_h u = (u(·+h)−u)/|h| (translations), first in all directions for interior regularity (R^N), and in tangential directions for boundary regularity (R^N_+), to obtain H^2 (and higher) regularity from H^1 weak solutions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Insert test functions built from D_h u (e.g., D_{−h}(D_h u)) into the weak formulation to obtain energy estimates for D_h u; use inequalities controlling D_{−h} by gradients (Proposition 9.3 / Lemma 9.6) and pass to the limit as h→0.

rubrics_metrics.name: Change-of-variables preserves ellipticity (boundary chart lemma)
rubrics_metrics.description: After flattening the boundary by a C^2 diffeomorphism H:Q→U, the pulled-back weak equation takes the form ∫_{Q+} ∑ a_{kℓ}(y) ∂_k w ∂_ℓ ψ = ∫_{Q+} ˜g ψ with a_{kℓ}∈C^1 and satisfying the ellipticity condition (Lemma 9.8).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This shows local boundary regularity reduces to an elliptic problem on Q_+, permitting the use of tangential translation techniques. The coefficients a_{kℓ} are built from Jacobians and satisfy uniform positivity because Jac H is nonsingular.

rubrics_metrics.name: Local (hypoelliptic) nature of regularity
rubrics_metrics.description: Regularity of u on a subdomain ω⊂⊂Ω depends only on the regularity of f on ω (not on f outside ω): if f∈C^∞(ω) then u∈C^∞(ω) even if f is irregular elsewhere (Remark 25).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although existence uses global information, smoothing properties are local. Use partition of unity and interior estimates to localize regularity proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technique for boundary estimates: partition of unity and local charts
rubrics_metrics.description: To obtain H^2-regularity for u on Ω, decompose u = ∑ θ_i u with θ_0 compactly supported in the interior and θ_i supported near boundary charts U_i; then apply interior regularity to θ_0 u and flattening + Q_+ estimates to each θ_i u.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Estimate local right-hand sides g arising from commutators with θ_i; control ∥θ_i u∥_{H^2} by ∥f∥_{L^2} using the chart-mapped elliptic estimates and Poincaré where needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maximum principle for the Dirichlet problem (Theorem 9.27)
rubrics_metrics.description: If f∈L^2(Ω) and u∈H^1(Ω)∩C(Ω) satisfies ∫(∇u·∇ϕ + u ϕ) = ∫ f ϕ for all ϕ∈H^1_0(Ω), then for all x∈Ω, min{ess inf_{∂Ω} u, ess inf_Ω f} ≤ u(x) ≤ max{ess sup_{∂Ω} u, ess sup_Ω f}.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof uses Stampacchia's truncation method: choose a suitable increasing truncation G and test with v=G(u−K) to compare u with boundary and forcing extremes. The statement uses essential sup/inf.
